commons:151721991.summary: In this small, glittering fragment a midwife in a striped headdress leans over the infant Christ, steadying him as he sits in a round basin, while a tall ewer stands ready at the left. The child already wears a cross-marked halo, so that a homely scene of washing becomes a sign of the Word truly made flesh. The piece is one of the few survivors of the mosaic cycle that Pope John VII placed in his oratory in Old St Peter's.
facts: The fragment comes from the oratory built by Pope John VII (705–707) in Old St Peter's Basilica; when the old basilica was demolished, a handful of its mosaics were saved, and this one is now kept in the Vatican Grottoes.
According to the Commons description, it originally sat directly above the central image of John VII with the Virgin, as part of a sequence of Nativity scenes.
The bathing of the newborn Christ is not told in the Gospels or apocrypha; it appears in Byzantine art from the 6th century and was linked by Christians with his later baptism.
commons:151721991.notes: Current location taken from the Commons category (Grotte vaticane); the photograph shows it in a modern display frame. Date follows John VII's pontificate.

cur:manuscripts-st-gall-gospels-crucifix.summary: Christ, with wide-open eyes and a great golden halo, stands before the cross, his body wrapped in a robe of red and purple bands that coil around him like interlace; Stephaton with the sponge and Longinus with the spear kneel close at either side, and two angels sit in the compartments above the cross-arm. The flat, symmetrical design turns the Passion into an icon of Christ's victory.
facts: According to e-codices, the Irish Gospel Book of St Gall was written and illuminated by Irish monks around 750 in Ireland and has 12 decorated pages.
It faces a page showing Christ at the Last Judgement, so that the Crucifixion and Second Coming are seen together at the end of the book.

cur:objects-athens-ivory-medallion-chris.summary: This small round medallion shows Christ in bust, with full curling hair and a short beard, clothed in a mantle and holding a book. Although worn, the face keeps a youthful, gentle expression typical of the 6th century. Medallions of this kind were set into larger objects, such as book covers or caskets, where the image of Christ crowned the composition.
facts: The museum catalogues it as BXM 835 and dates it to the 6th century.
A similar medallion bust of Christ held by angels crowns the upper panel of the Barberini Ivory in the Louvre, showing how such images were used (comparison).
